You've hit on a fascinating tension. Evolutionary psychology explains how we protect our genes, but it doesn't care about society, the economy, or the state.

When you shift the lens from the individual to the government or larger ecosystem, the entire purpose of marriage and mating gets turned on its head. Historically, governments and societies didn't care about your raw attraction or your deep pair-bonding chemicals. To the macro-system, mating is about stability, resource allocation, and citizenship management.

Here is how the game changes when the larger ecosystem takes control of human mating.

1. Mating as a Macro-Economic Strategy

From a state perspective, mating is the ultimate structural stabilizer. For thousands of years, marriage was less about two individuals falling in love and more about two families forming an economic and political merger.

  • Property and Wealth Inheritance: Governments need a clear, legally binding framework to track who owns what and who it passes to when someone dies. Without organized pair-bonding, wealth distribution becomes chaotic, leading to civil disputes and unstable tax bases.
  • The Division of Labor: Society relies on a predictable unit to handle both productive labor (working the fields, the factories, or coding at a desk) and reproductive labor (raising the next generation of taxpayers and workers). The domestic partnership acts as a self-funding micro-corporation that manages these roles without the government having to step in and fund collective childcare or daily survival infrastructure.

2. Managing Social Friction (The "Unmated Male" Problem)

From a governance standpoint, a society full of completely unmoored, competing individuals is incredibly volatile. If human mating were left purely to the "raw attraction" algorithms you mentioned earlier, it would likely result in hyper-competition—where a tiny percentage of high-status individuals capture all the romantic interest, leaving a massive population of unmated individuals.

Historically, governments and religious institutions pushed monogamy not necessarily out of a moral breakthrough, but as a peace-keeping policy.

The Stabilization Effect: Monogamous cultural norms effectively "democratized" access to partners. By capping the number of partners a high-status individual could legally or socially have, society reduced the number of disenfranchised, high-testosterone young males. Historically, large populations of young, unmated men with low social stakes are the primary drivers of internal crime, rebellion, and systemic instability.

3. The State's Obsession with the Birth Rate

To a government, the ultimate output of human mating is the demographic pyramid.

A healthy ecosystem requires a predictable supply of new humans to replace the older ones. When individuals choose partners purely based on personal happiness or short-term desire, they might choose not to reproduce at all.

[Individual Strategy] ---------> Focuses on: Personal Fulfillment / Gene Survival
                                      vs.
[Government Strategy] ---------> Focuses on: Sustainable Demographics / Labor Supply

Because of this, states have historically used a massive array of levers to manipulate personal mating choices into alignment with public policy:

  • Tax Incentives: Offering financial breaks for married couples and child dependents.
  • Legal Frameworks: Restricting or granting privileges (like healthcare access, housing rights, and immigration visas) based on official relationship status.
  • Cultural Narrative: Using state media, religion, or social pressure to frame family creation as a civic duty.

The Modern Disconnect

The friction we see in modern dating often stems from the fact that these two forces are currently pulling in opposite directions.

For the first time in human history, effective birth control, financial independence for women, and online dating apps have decoupled mating from both state-enforced economic necessity and traditional community oversight. We are back to running our raw, individual evolutionary software at scale—which is exactly why modern governments are panicking about crashing birth rates and shifting social structures. The individual is optimizing for the self, while the macro-system is losing its predictable foundation.

The Two Dragons: Emotion and Logistics

You hit on the two most critical failure points of trying to scale human relationships beyond a 1:1 ratio:

1. The Emotional Dragon: Jealousy and Ego

Jealousy isn't just a minor insecurity; evolutionarily, it is a deeply wired panic response designed to protect resources and genetic certainty. Taming it is one thing, but as you pointed out, the real threat is the human ego.

  • To date multiple people ethically and healthily, a person’s ego has to be incredibly quiet.
  • If a shred of narcissism, control, or a desire for validation drives the dynamic, it instantly becomes toxic.
  • You have to manage not only your own ego but also the ego demands of every single person within that network. If one person feels deprioritized, the whole system destabilizes.

2. The Operational Dragon: The Complexity Multiplier

Even if you somehow managed to completely eliminate jealousy, you are still left with a brutal project-management problem. Human beings do not scale linearly; they scale exponentially in terms of complexity.

$$Complexity \propto N^2$$

Where $N$ is the number of people involved. When you add a person, you aren’t just adding one more schedule; you are adding their emotional baggage, their daily stressors, their communication style, and their demands on your most finite assets: time, focused attention, and mental energy.

Dating multiple people casually or transparently can be healthy if it prevents you from prematurely attaching to the wrong person out of loneliness, or if it helps you understand what you actually want. But as a sustainable lifestyle? For the vast majority of people, the massive drain on mental bandwidth and the constant exposure to emotional friction (both from within and from outside judgment) makes the cost far outweigh the benefits.

Recognizing that you don't want to fight that dragon right now—or ever—isn't a limitation. It’s strategic resource allocation. Choosing to protect your time, energy, and peace of mind from that kind of exponential complexity is probably one of the healthiest individual choices you can make.

Look at how the system behaves as the parameter along the bottom axis ($r$) moves from left to right:

  • On the left, at a low baseline, the system is a single, clean, perfectly predictable line (stable equilibrium).
